An Investigation of Body Appreciation, Ethnic Identity, and Eating Disorder Symptoms in Black Women
Journal of Black Psychology 2015, Vol. 41(1) 3–25 © The Author(s) 2013 Reprints and permissions: sagepub.com/journalsPermissions.nav DOI: 10.1177/0095798413502671 jbp.sagepub.com
Elizabeth W. Cotter1, Nichole R. Kelly1, Karen S. Mitchell2,3, and Suzanne E. Mazzeo1

Positive body image, such as body appreciation or acceptance, has gone largely unexamined in women of color in comparison with more pathological body attitudes. In an effort to promote and extend positive body image research, this study examined the reliability and validity of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS) in Black college women, as well as the relation between ethnic identity and body appreciation. Participants were 228 Black college women (M age = 19.89, SD = 4.57). The relation between BAS scores and measures of appearance evaluation, self-esteem, Western beauty ideal internalization, eating disordered behavior, and teasing was examined to investigate convergent and divergent validity. Results supported the construct validity of this measure. Similar to previous research, a confirmatory factor analysis supported a unidimensional factor structure. Ethnic identity was moderately, positively associated with body appreciation. Western beauty ideal internalization mediated the relation between ethnic identity and eating, weight, and shape concerns. Overall, findings support the use of the BAS with Black college women.

Body image is a complex construct that encompasses a person's thoughts, feelings, perceptions, and attitudes regarding his or her body. The majority of research related to body image has focused on negative aspects of this construct, such as body dissatisfaction (Cash, 2002; Stewart & Williamson, 2004) and weight concern (Fitzsimmons & Bardone-Cone, 2011; Luce & Crowther, 1999). Examination of these constructs is warranted, as poor body image has been linked to a number of important outcomes, including negative affect, eating disorder symptoms, and threshold eating disorders (Hrabosky et al., 2009; Stice, 2001; Stice, Mazotti, Wiebel, & Agras, 2000). However, few studies have focused on more positive aspects of body image, such as body esteem or body appreciation. This focus is crucial, as positive body image is also associated with important outcomes, including increased acceptance of bodily imperfections, engagement in healthy self-care behaviors, and the ability to deconstruct unrealistic media images (Frisen & Holmqvist, 2010; Wood-Barcalow, Tylka, & Augustus-Horvath, 2010), the latter being a critical component of empirically supported eating disorder prevention programming (Stice, Chase, Stormer, & Appel, 2001).

Research generally indicates that Black women tend to be more satisfied with their bodies than White women (Gluck & Geliebter, 2002; Kronenfeld, Reba-Harrelson, Van Holle, Reyes, & Bulik, 2010). A 2006 meta-analysis found that Black women reported slightly less body dissatisfaction than White and Hispanic women, with the greatest differences seen between White and Black women during adolescence and young adulthood (Grabe & Hyde, 2006). Previous studies also have found that Black women generally prefer larger body sizes, are less likely to idealize thin frames, and are less likely to see themselves as overweight (Celio, Zabinski, & Wilfley, 2002; Gordon, Castro, Sitnikov, & Holm-Denoma, 2010; Kronenfeld et al., 2010; Paeratakul, White, Williamson, Ryan, & Bray, 2002; Webb, Warren-Findlow, Chou, & Adams, 2013) compared with White women. Qualitative research has indicated that, contrary to the thin ideals found in mainstream media, larger frames are viewed as more physically appealing and attractive among Black adolescents (Barroso, Peters, Jones Johnson, Kelder, & Jefferson, 2010). Perhaps because of these differences, Black young adults report lower rates of dieting than their White peers (Field et al., 2007).

Despite lower body dissatisfaction, Black women are not immune to body image and eating concerns. While some studies have found that Black women experience less eating disorder symptomatology than White women (Gordon et al., 2010; Napolitano & Himes, 2011; Sanchez-Johnsen et al., 2004; Striegel-Moore et al., 2003), other studies have found no differences in eating disorder symptomatology between these two groups (Franko, Becker, Thomas, & Herzog, 2007; Mitchell & Mazzeo, 2004; Striegel-Moore, Wilfley, Pike, Dohm, & Fairburn, 2000; Wilfley, Schwartz, Spurrell, & Fairburn, 1997). Indeed, an investigation conducted with a nationally representative sample from the United States found no differences in eating disorder prevalence across racial groups (Hudson, Hiripi, Pope, & Kessler, 2007). Moreover, a study of eating disorder prevalence in Black college women indicated that 23% were symptomatic (Mulholland & Mintz, 2001), although none met criteria for a threshold eating disorder. Thus, Black women do experience a range of body image attitudes and concerns, and reliable measures are needed to assess these accurately. Unfortunately, the majority of extant body image measures have been normed on samples of primarily White women (Kelly et al., 2012). Therefore, an important next step in this research involves examining the validity of existing body image related measures in Black samples.

When investigating the validity of body image measures in Black women, it is important to consider cultural factors relevant to the development of body image attitudes among this ethnic group. These cultural factors might include acculturative stress, experiences of racism and oppression, and ethnic identity (Henrickson, Crowther, & Harrington, 2010; Kempa & Thomas, 2000; Levine & Smolak, 2010; Perez, Voelz, Pettit, & Joiner, 2002). For example, Rogers Wood and Petrie (2010) found that ethnic identity was inversely related to the internalization of societal beauty ideals. Similarly, Schooler, Ward, Merriwether, and Caruthers (2004) found that ethnic identity predicted healthier body image in Black women. Qualitative research also suggested a positive association between a stronger racial/ethnic identity and body satisfaction (Hesse-Biber, Livingstone, Ramirez, Barko, & Johnson, 2010).

These findings are consistent with the sociocultural model of disordered eating (see Fitzsimmons-Craft, 2011, for a review), which posits that body image concerns and eating disordered behavior stem from increasing pressures within Western culture to achieve extreme thinness. Women might experience these pressures from media (Stice & Shaw, 1994), friends, and family (Stice, 1998). Using this sociocultural perspective, ethnic identity might protect individuals from the development of body image concerns by

weakening identification with the majority culture's thin-ideal. Specifically, a connection to a Black ethnic group that is more accepting and appreciative of larger body shapes might serve to inhibit internalization of a thin-ideal and therefore reduce body image concerns and eating pathology. Indeed, a growing body of research suggests that thin ideal internalization is a major risk factor for eating disordered behavior and body image disturbance (Stice, 2002), yet currently there is little understanding of how cultural differences might influence this association.

The current study examined body appreciation and its association with ethnic identity in Black college women. Independently examining the psychometric properties of this construct in Black women is important, as appreciation for one's body might be less dependent on weight or achieving the thin ideal in this population. This study uses the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005), which was originally developed and validated using four independent samples of predominately White, middle- to upper-class college women, with results from the validation study supporting a unidimensional factor structure for this 13-item measure. Although a small number of other positively oriented body image measures do exist (e.g., Body Esteem Scale; Franzoi & Shields, 1984), these generally examine satisfaction with specific aspects of appearance, as opposed to a more holistic form of body appreciation, involving respect and acceptance of one's body. Thus, the BAS was selected as the most appropriate measure for the current study.

More research is needed to examine the factor structure of the BAS in ethnically and culturally diverse populations. Although research with samples from Austria and the United States found evidence for a unidimensional factor structure (Avalos et al., 2005; Swami, Stieger, Haubner, & Voracek, 2008), a study using the BAS in a sample of Malay women suggested two stable factors (Swami & Chamorro-Premuzic, 2008). Furthermore, the bulk of research involving the BAS in the United States has involved primarily White samples (Avalos et al., 2005; Iannantuono & Tylka, 2012; Satinsky, Reece, Dennis, Sanders, & Bardzell, 2012) and has not examined potential ethnic differences in body appreciation and its correlates. Finally, it is imperative to examine whether body appreciation in Black women is associated with eating disorder risk factors identified among primarily White samples, including weight-related teasing (Grilo & Masheb, 2005; Libbey, Story, Neumark-Sztainer, & Boutelle, 2008) and dieting (Hoerr, Bokram, Lugo, Bivins, & Keast, 2002; Neumark-Sztainer et al., 2006). These data could inform prevention and intervention efforts that are culturally relevant for Black women living in the United States.

The goals of the present study were to (a) validate the BAS (Avalos et al., 2005) in Black college women and (b) examine the role of ethnic identity in body appreciation. It was hypothesized that a confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) of the BAS in a sample of Black undergraduate women would support a unidimensional factor structure. Second, it was hypothesized that the BAS scores of Black undergraduate women would be positively correlated with appearance satisfaction and general self-esteem, providing evidence for the scale's construct validity. Third, it was hypothesized that the BAS scores of Black college women would be negatively correlated with Western beauty ideal internalization, dieting, eating disordered behavior, and weight-related teasing, providing further evidence of construct validity. Fourth, it was hypothesized that higher BAS scores would be related to higher identification with one's ethnic group and lower levels of eating disorder symptoms. Fifth, it was hypothesized that the relations between ethnic identity and body appreciation, eating concerns, shape concerns, and weight concerns would each be mediated by Western beauty ideal internalization.

Participants were 228 undergraduate Black female college students (M age = 19.89, SD = 4.57) at a large, urban university in the Mid-Atlantic. Approximately 52% of the student body at this university is White, and 19% is Black. Most participants were first-year students (n = 135, 59.2%), followed by sophomores (n = 52, 22.8%), juniors (n = 30, 13.2%), seniors (n = 10, 4.4%), and graduate students (n = 1, 0.4%). Self-reported height and weight data were used to calculate body mass index (BMI), an estimate of body fat percentage (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2011). Mean BMI was 24.71 (SD = 6.04), which is just below the overweight range (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2011). Measures were administered through a secure website called SONA Systems, an online data collection program maintained by the university. Participants were recruited from a Psychology 101 Participant Pool, as well as other psychology courses. Participation in this pool is one way in which students can fulfill a course requirement.
Body Appreciation Scale. The BAS (Avalos et al., 2005) includes 13 items rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Scores are

averaged to obtain an overall body appreciation score, with higher scores reflecting greater body appreciation (e.g., "I take a positive attitude toward my body"). Avalos et al. reported evidence of construct validity for this scale and demonstrated the expected associations with body esteem, optimism, psychological well-being, body shame, and body surveillance. Test–retest (3-week, r = .90) and internal consistency (α = .91-.94) also were reported by the scale developers (Avalos et al., 2005). Cronbach's coefficient alpha in the current sample was .92.

The Multidimensional Body Self-Relations Questionnaire, Appearance Evaluation Subscale (MBSRQ-AE; Brown, Cash, & Mikulka, 1990; Cash, 2000). The MBSRQ-AE subscale measures a respondent's global evaluation of his or her appearance (e.g., "I like my looks just the way they are"). It includes seven items rated on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (definitely disagree) to 5 (definitely agree). Item scores are summed and averaged; higher overall means indicate greater appearance satisfaction. Evidence of the subscale's validity is supported via its associations in the expected directions with selfesteem, body part satisfaction, depression, and bulimic symptoms (Petrie, Rogers, Johnson, & Diehl, 1996; Petrie, Tripp, & Harvey, 2002). Cash, Morrow, Hrabosky, and Perry (2004) reported adequate Cronbach's coefficient alphas in samples including Black women (α = .83-.93). Cronbach's coefficient alpha in the current sample was .85.

The Multigroup Ethnic Identity Measure (MEIM; Phinney, 1992). The MEIM is a 15-item measure of ethnic identity (e.g., "I have a strong sense of belonging to my own ethnic group") consisting of two subscales: (a) ethnic identity search and (b) affirmation, belonging, and commitment. Items 1 to 12 are rated on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Items 13 to 15 are used strictly for purposes of ethnic/racial categorization. Phinney recommends obtaining a mean of Items 1 to 12 for an overall score. A review of past research on the MEIM provides evidence of validity in Black samples via its relations in the expected directions with self-esteem, Afrocentrism, and Afrocentric values (Cokley, 2005; Goodstein & Ponterotto, 1997). Past research also suggests that the MEIM yields internally consistent scores in Black samples (α = .70-.81; Cokley, 2005; Goodstein & Ponterotto, 1997). Cronbach's coefficient alpha in the current sample was .82.

The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES; Rosenberg, 1965). This measure of general self-esteem (e.g., "I feel that I have a number of good qualities") includes 10 items ranked on a 4-point scale ranging from 1 (strongly agree) to 4 (strongly disagree). Evidence of validity in Black samples has been

demonstrated via the scale's association with satisfaction with life (Utsey, Ponterotto, Reynolds, & Cancelli, 2000) and positive regard for Blacks (Rowley, Sellers, Chavous, & Smith, 1998). Past research also demonstrated adequate internal consistency in a Black college sample (α = .87; Rowley et al., 1998). Cronbach's coefficient alpha for the current sample was .87.

The Sociocultural Attitudes Toward Appearance Scale–3, Internalization-General Subscale (SATAQ-3; Thompson, van den Berg, Roehrig, Guarda, & Heinberg, 2004). The SATAQ-3 is a measure of societal influences on body image and eating disturbances. The Internalization-General subscale measures endorsement and acceptance of messages in the media promoting unrealistic beauty ideals (e.g., "I've felt pressure from TV or magazines to have a perfect body"). It includes nine items ranked on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (definitely disagree) to 5 (definitely agree). Thompson et al. demonstrated evidence of this subscale's validity via its associations in the expected directions with drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction, and ideal body internalization. Adequate internal consistency has been demonstrated in a sample of Black college women (α = .74; Falconer & Neville, 2000). Cronbach's coefficient alpha in the current study was .91.

Eating Attitudes Test-26, Dieting Subscale (EAT-26; Garner, Olmsted, Bohr, & Garfinkel, 1982). This is a 13-item subscale of the EAT-26 that measures attitudes toward dieting, as well as dietary behaviors (e.g., "I engage in dieting behavior"). Items are ranked on a 6-point scale ranging from 0 (never, rarely, sometimes) to 3 (always). A total score is derived from a sum of the composite items. Research has supported the convergent validity of the EAT-26 in a sample of Black women via its positive associations with purging, weight cycling, and interference with social relationships (Hoerr et al., 2002). Koenig and Wasserman (1995) reported adequate internal consistency (α = .86) of the Dieting subscale in a sample of college women. Cronbach's coefficient alpha for the Dieting subscale in the current sample was .83.

Eating Disorders Self-Examination-Questionnaire (EDE-Q; Fairburn & Beglin, 1994). The EDE-Q assesses the frequency of eating disordered behaviors and attitudes occurring within the previous 28 days and consists of 36 items. The EDE-Q includes four subscales: Restraint (EDE-Q-R, "Have you tried to avoid eating foods which you like in order to influence your shape or weight?"), Weight Concern (EDE-Q-WC, "Have you had a definite fear that you might gain weight or become fat?"), Shape Concern (EDE-Q-SC, "Have you definitely wanted your stomach to be flat?"), and Eating Concern (EDE-Q-EC, "Have you eaten in secret?"). Additional questions (Goldfein, Devlin,

& Kamenetz, 2005) were added to this measure to provide examples of binge eating episodes (vs. overeating episodes) to enhance the accuracy of respondents' recall of these symptoms. Evidence of the scale's concurrent validity has been demonstrated via its strong association with the interview format of the EDE (Mond, Hay, Rodgers, Owen, & Beumont, 2004). Past research indicates that the EDE-Q's items demonstrate excellent 2-week temporal stability, with coefficients ranging from .81 to .94 (Luce & Crowther, 1999). Research has also demonstrated evidence of internal consistency in a sample of Black college women (α = .79-.91; Kelly, Cotter, & Mazzeo, 2012). Cronbach's coefficient alphas in the current sample were as follows: Restraint (.82), Eating Concern (.82), Shape Concern (.92), Weight Concern (.89), and Global (.96).

The Physical Appearance–Related Testing Scale, Weight/Size Teasing Subscale (PARTS; Thompson, Fabian, Moulton, Dunn, & Altabe, 1991). The 12-item weight/size teasing subscale measures experiences of being teased because of one's body size (e.g., "Were you ridiculed as a child about being overweight?"). Items are ranked on a 5-point scale ranging from 1 (never) to 5 (frequently). Thompson et al. demonstrated evidence of this subscale's validity in undergraduate women via its associations in the expected directions with drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction, and discrepancies between ideal and actual figure ratings. Thompson et al. also reported high internal consistency (α = .91) and 2-week test–retest reliability (r = .86). Cronbach's coefficient alpha for the current sample was .93.
Demographics Questionnaire. This questionnaire was created by the researchers and asks participants to report their age, year in school, ethnicity, gender, height, and weight.

Descriptive statistics were calculated using SPSS 19.0. Differences between the current sample and previously published results were examined using independent samples t tests. Evidence of construct validity was examined using Pearson correlation coefficients. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and CFA using Mplus version 6.0 (Muthén & Muthén, 1998-2011) were conducted to examine the factor structure of the BAS in this sample of Black college women. The CFA model was evaluated using the comparative fit index (CFI), standardized root mean square residual (SRMR), and root mean squared error of approximation (RMSEA) indices. Mediation analyses were completed using an SPSS macro (Preacher & Hayes, 2004), which used a nonparametric bootstrapping approach involving 5,000 bootstrapped

The current sample also endorsed lower average scores on the EDE-Q-R, t(949) = 4.53, p < .001, and the EDE-Q-EC, t(949) = 3.15, p = .002, than the sample of undergraduate women examined by Luce, Crowther, and Pole (2008). A preliminary EFA was conducted to explore BAS factor structure in the current sample, and two factors emerged with eigenvalues greater than 1. However, on closer examination of the factor loadings, only one item loaded onto the second factor, indicating that a unidimensional factor was most appropriate; this was supported by a scree plot. Next, a single CFA factor model was estimated to confirm this unidimensional factor structure. The model provided an adequate fit to the data (χ2 = 185.02, df = 65, CFI = .94, SRMR = .05, RMSEA = .09). The fit of the model in the current sample was comparable to that reported in the development sample (Avalos et al., 2005). All factor loadings were significant and ranged from .42 to .91 (see Table 2).

Thus, these results support the unidimensional nature of this measure among Black women.

See Table 3 for correlations between study variables. The BAS was positively correlated with measures of appearance evaluation (MBSRQ-AE) and general self-esteem (RSES). Specifically, participants who reported greater appreciation of their bodies also reported higher satisfaction with their overall appearance and greater general self-esteem. In contrast, the BAS was negatively correlated with measures of Western ideal beauty internalization (SATAQ-3 Internalization-General), dieting (EAT-26 Dieting), past experiences of weight-related teasing (PARTS Weight/Size), BMI, and eating disordered symptoms, including dietary restraint (EDE-Q-R), eating concern (EDE-Q-EC), shape concern (EDE-Q-SC), and weight concern (EDE-Q-WC). Thus, individuals with lower body appreciation scores reported higher levels of dieting, more weight-related teasing, higher BMIs, and greater disordered eating pathology.

As hypothesized, ethnic identity, as measured by the MEIM, was positively associated with body appreciation (BAS); women with higher ethnic identification also reported greater body appreciation. Ethnic identity also had a moderate, positive relation with self-esteem (RSES) and a small, positive association with appearance evaluation (MBSRQ AE). In addition, MEIM scores had small, but significant, negative associations with Western ideal beauty internalization (SATAQ-3 Internalization-General), eating concerns (EDE-Q-EC), shape concerns (EDE-Q-SC), and weight concerns (EDE-Q-WC). MEIM scores were not significantly associated with any eating disordered behaviors assessed by the EDE-Q, including binge eating, vomiting, dietary restriction, laxative use, diuretic use, and excessive exercise.

The potential role of Western beauty ideal internalization as a mediator between ethnic identity and body appreciation and eating disorder pathology was tested using a nonparametric boot-strapping approach recommended by Preacher and Hayes (2004). We used 5,000 bootstrapped resamples to test the significance of the indirect effect of ethnic identity (MEIM), via the potential mediating role of Western beauty ideal internalization (SATAQ-3 Internalization-General), on body appreciation (BAS), eating concern (EDE-Q-EC), shape concern (EDE-Q-SC), and weight concern (EDE-Q-WC). The vast majority of research investigating body image and eating disorder symptoms has examined negative aspects of body image, such as

dissatisfaction. However, recently researchers have begun to define and explain factors that may protect individuals from eating disorder symptoms, such as positive body image or body appreciation (Avalos et al., 2005; Frisen & Holmqvist, 2010; Holmqvist & Frisen, 2012; Wood-Barcalow et al., 2010). It is important to investigate these positive aspects of body image, as they are associated with reduced eating disorder psychopathology and internalization of media ideals, and increased selfesteem (Avalos et al., 2005; Molloy & Herzberger, 1998; Wood-Barcalow et al., 2010). Nonetheless, like most measures of eating disorder symptoms and risk factors (see Kelly, Mitchell, et al., 2012, for a review), studies examining the psychometric properties of the BAS, a measure of body appreciation, have included primarily White women (Avalos et al., 2005). Although this measure has been validated with women from Austria (Swami et al., 2008) and Malaysia (Swami & Chamorro-Premuzic, 2008), the relevance of body appreciation and its associations with disordered eating pathology among Black women remained unknown. To facilitate use of this measure within this ethnic group, the current study provided psychometric data for the BAS using a sample of Black college women. Associations among body appreciation, ethnic identity, and disordered eating pathology were also examined.

Consistent with samples composed primarily of White women (Avalos et al., 2005), the current study found that the BAS yields both reliable and valid scores within a sample of Black women in the United States. Specifically, the measure yielded internally consistent scores, and the original unidimensional factor structure was supported. Furthermore, the BAS total score demonstrated good construct validity as evidenced by its significant associations with several measures of eating- and weight-related constructs, as well as self-esteem. Specifically, Black women with greater appreciation for their bodies also reported higher self-esteem and body satisfaction. Higher body appreciation also was linked to less history of weightrelated teasing, lower eating, weight and shape concerns, and lower Western beauty ideal internalization. The current sample also displayed higher body appreciation and lower levels of dietary restraint and eating concerns than previously published samples of primarily White undergraduates (Avalos et al., 2005; Luce et al., 2008), in line with past research suggesting that Black women are less susceptible to body image concerns than their White peers (Gluck & Geliebter, 2002; Kronenfeld et al., 2010; Von Holle, Wei, & Nickerson, 2010).

Body appreciation also had a moderate, negative relation with BMI. Previous research has suggested that Black women are more accepting of overweight than their White peers (Grabe & Hyde, 2006; Kronenfeld et al.,

2010). Black women are also less likely to view themselves as overweight or to view a higher BMI as problematic in comparison with BMI-matched White women (Paeratakul et al., 2002; Williamson et al., 2000). However, findings from the current study suggest that BMI is relevant to appearance satisfaction and shape and weight concern in Black college women.

The current results support the use of the BAS with Black women. Although the cross-sectional design of this study precludes any conclusions regarding the potential role of body appreciation as a protective factor against the development of eating disorders among Black women, findings indicate that body appreciation is strongly associated with a number of important risk factors. For example, a recent longitudinal study (Stice, Marti, & Durant, 2011) identified body dissatisfaction and dieting behavior as two of the strongest predictors of eating disorders among adolescent girls, and both body dissatisfaction and drive for thinness predicted binge eating among Black college women (Napolitano & Himes, 2011). Given its association with appearance satisfaction, dieting, and other risk factors within the current sample, body appreciation might play an important protective role in the development of eating disorders and could have implications for prevention and treatment. However, additional longitudinal research is needed to clarify such temporal links, particularly among Black women.

It also is important to examine cultural factors that might be relevant to the development of positive body image as well as eating disorders among Black women. To that end, the current study examined the link between ethnic identity and body appreciation, as well as other eating- and weight-related constructs. Similar to previous research (Hesse-Biber et al., 2010; Rogers Wood & Petrie, 2010; Schooler et al., 2004), women who identified more strongly with their ethnic group were also more likely to appreciate their bodies, and less likely to internalize the thin ideal, or to report concerns with their eating, shape, and weight. Importantly, these variables were weakly to moderately correlated, suggesting that ethnic identity explains only a portion of participants' body appreciation. Western beauty ideal internalization also mediated the association between ethnic identity and eating, shape, and weight concern. As such, and consistent with the sociocultural model, a strong ethnic identity may protect some Black women from believing that achieving mainstream beauty ideals will improve their quality of life, which, in turn, may prevent the onset of eating disorder symptoms and risk factors.

Consistent with one previous study (Rogers Wood & Petrie, 2010), ethnic identity in the current investigation was not directly associated with maladaptive disordered eating behaviors, including bulimic symptoms, binge eating, or dieting. However, research regarding the link between ethnic identity and disordered eating is mixed. For example, Shuttlesworth and Zotter (2011)

found that a stronger ethnic identity was associated with lower levels of binge eating and bulimic behavior, although not with global disordered eating pathology. In light of the limitations associated with cross-sectional, selfreport data, additional qualitative and prospective research is needed to clarify how various racial and cultural factors influence body appreciation and disordered eating pathology among Black women.

The salience of various racial and cultural variables might depend, in part, on individual's developmental stage. The transition to college is a particularly relevant time to evaluate the associations among ethnic identity, body appreciation, and disordered eating. In particular, young Black women entering predominantly White colleges might experience conflict between their ethnic identity and the majority culture's beauty ideals, which could increase their vulnerability to body dissatisfaction and related symptoms (Henrickson et al., 2010). Thus, as others have noted (Rogers Wood & Petrie, 2010; Shuttlesworth & Zotter, 2011), the college campus can provide a unique and powerful setting in which to prevent disordered eating pathology among Black women. Specifically, eating disorder intervention and preventions efforts could focus on helping Black women promote and/or maintain their connection with the beliefs, values, and cultural practices of their ethnic group, particularly those that relate to body appreciation. Targeted efforts to strengthen ethnic identity might prevent the onset of or reduce the severity of disordered eating behavior and attitudes, while also promoting body appreciation by reducing internalization of the thin ideal.

The current study's outcomes should be considered in light of several limitations, including the reliance on self-report measures, which introduces concerns regarding response bias. Future research should utilize naturalistic or observational designs, in conjunction with self-report, to enhance understanding of the complexities of situation-based body image and ethnic identity, as well as their interactions with one another. Self-reported height and weight is a related limitation in the current study. Previous research has found that women have a tendency to underreport their weight, particularly if they are overweight or obese (Elgar & Stewart, 2008; Ezzati, Martin, Skjold, Vander Hoorn, & Murray, 2006; Shields, Gorber, & Tremblay, 2008; Stommel & Schoenborn, 2009). However, discrepancies between self-report and measured weight are generally small (about 5 lbs or 1.16 BMI points, on average, among women) and thus unlikely to have a significant statistical influence on the current study's results. Future research should examine how body image appreciation influences the accuracy of self-reported height and weight; such research could extend previous work that has identified a link between overweight and obesity and body dissatisfaction (Mond, Van den Berg, Boutelle, Hannan, & Neumark-Sztainer, 2011; Schwartz & Brownell, 2004).

The use of a college sample is another potential limitation, given the relatively high educational attainment within this group. However, previous research has identified the strongest between-group ethnic differences in body satisfaction during the college years (Grabe & Hyde, 2006; Roberts, Cash, Feingold, & Johnson, 2006; Wildes, Emery, & Simons, 2001). Future research examining body appreciation among community and clinical samples, as well as among women with more diverse age and educational backgrounds, is necessary. Age has also been identified as a significant moderator of ethnic differences in body dissatisfaction, and body image is known to change both across the lifespan and during various life events (Grabe & Hyde, 2006; Roberts et al., 2006). However, it remains unclear whether age has a similar association with body appreciation, and future longitudinal designs are critical in elucidating such processes. Finally, this research did not take into account certain aspects of appearance particularly salient to Black women that might influence body appreciation, such as skin color (Bond & Cash, 1992; Buchanan, Fischer, Tokar, & Yoder, 2008; Falconer & Neville, 2000), facial features, or hair (Altabe, 1998; Patton, 2006; Thompson, 2006).

Despite the noted limitations, the current study extends previous research by providing psychometric information for a measure of body appreciation using a sample of Black women (as suggested by Avalos et al., 2005). Results provide preliminary justification for interventions that reduce thin ideal internalization while promoting body appreciation and a stronger Black ethnic identity.
